descriptions.title: Why xxhash and not MD5/SHA-256
descriptions.body: Duplicate detection needs to fingerprint potentially millions of files, so the hash must be fast, not cryptographically secure — these files are not being protected against a forging adversary, just compared for equality. FileHQ uses xxhash64, a non-cryptographic hash that is many times faster than MD5 or SHA-256 and more than sufficient to decide 'are these two files byte-identical?'. The cost that matters here is disk I/O, and xxhash keeps the CPU from becoming the bottleneck while a terabyte of data streams past.

descriptions.title: The three-phase hashing pipeline (why singletons are never read)
descriptions.body: Hashing every file would mean reading every byte on the drive — wasteful, because a file with a unique size cannot have a duplicate. hash_candidates() exploits this in three stages. Phase 1: SELECT size_bytes ... GROUP BY size_bytes HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 finds only sizes shared by two or more files. Phase 2: those candidates get a cheap partial hash (first + last 64KB); a unique partial hash clears a file. Phase 3: only files that still collide on the partial hash are read in full. The result: the vast majority of files are never fully read, turning an O(all bytes) job into one that touches only genuine duplicate suspects.

descriptions.title: Read-first, write-never (until approved)
descriptions.body: FileHQ's core promise is that indexing is non-destructive. The scanner, categorizer, hasher, and duplicate finder only read the filesystem and write to filehq.db — they never touch a user's files. The only modules that mutate the disk are the dedup executor and the organizer executor, and both default to dry_run=True. When invoked through Naya, the bridge additionally requires approved=True, which is only set after the owner says 'you may proceed' in the same message. Every real mutation is then recorded in the operations table with a batch_id and undo_path so it can be reversed.

descriptions.title: SQLite as the whole datastore (WAL + busy_timeout)
descriptions.body: There is no server database — the entire index, duplicate map, operation log, task schedule, and exception rules live in one file, db/filehq.db. get_connection() opens it with journal_mode=WAL (so the dashboard can read while a scan writes), foreign_keys=ON (so duplicate_members can't dangle off a deleted group), and busy_timeout=5000 (so concurrent writers wait rather than error). The catalogue currently holds ~2.86 million file rows, which SQLite handles comfortably with the size/hash/category indexes defined in the schema.

descriptions.title: Config that defers to Naya
descriptions.body: FileHQ keeps its own config/config.yaml (categories, skip rules, archive layout, scheduler intervals) but deliberately does not own the most important runtime value — which drive to scan. load_config() calls into naya_db.get_config('personal.default_scan_drive') and overrides primary_drive with whatever Naya has stored. This is the merge in microcosm: FileHQ provides the capability, Naya provides the identity and the user-facing settings, and the engine bends to the parent rather than holding a competing source of truth.

descriptions.title: Two ways into the engine: REST and direct DB
descriptions.body: filehq_bridge.py talks to FileHQ two ways. For actions and live job state it makes HTTP calls to the FastAPI app (_get/_post/_put/_delete). For fast, read-only reporting — counts, largest files, category and drive breakdowns, filename search — it skips HTTP entirely and opens the SQLite file directly in read-only mode (sqlite3.connect('file:...?mode=ro', uri=True)). This keeps Naya's conversational answers snappy (no web round-trip) while still routing anything that changes state through the API, which is where the approval guards live.
